about: Static mock Wave corpus for the wave-client-for-emacs mock server.
Ten mock users on localhost, each with a fixed set of interests; a user only creates, joins or replies to waves on topics they hold.
Topics come from the owner's research notes (paths under topics.*.notes are relative to the site root).
Some waves are discussions of a real Hacker News story: only its id, title, date, points and comment-tree shape were used (hn_snapshot).
No HN comment text and no HN usernames were fetched into this file; every blip is original text written for this corpus.
Blip count per HN wave = clamp(4, 15, 2 + round(sqrt(comments) / 2)); reply depth never exceeds the story's max_depth.
read_through: the user has read the wave up to and including that blip (null = never opened).

waves.title: Google Wave is the new X-Windows
waves.creator: frank@localhost

blips.author: frank@localhost
lines: Read this over coffee. The comparison is fun but I am not sure it holds.
X shipped a protocol and a reference server first; Wave shipped a client and a promise.

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: It holds in one way: both put the interesting state on the server and let thin clients draw it.
That is exactly why an Emacs client is plausible at all.

blips.author: dave@localhost
lines: Plausible, sure, but X had a wire spec you could implement in a weekend. The Wave docs are mostly screenshots.

blips.author: frank@localhost
lines: The federation draft is real though. Operations over XMPP, a spec for the document model.
Not a weekend, but not vapor either.

blips.author: bob@localhost
lines: Meanwhile I just want the scrollbar to behave.

waves.title: What problems does Google Wave solve?
waves.creator: erin@localhost

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: Honest question for the group, since half of us have sandbox accounts now.
What do we actually use it for that email plus a wiki did not already cover?

blips.author: charlie@localhost
lines: Meeting notes. Four people typing into one blip during the call, then replies threaded under the decisions.

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: Same here. Live typing turns out to matter more than I expected; you see the half-sentence and answer the question before it is asked.

blips.author: bob@localhost
lines: For me it is the playback. Joining late and scrubbing through how a doc got to its current shape is genuinely new.

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: Fair. Playback is the one feature I cannot fake with email.

blips.author: frank@localhost
lines: You can fake it with version control, but nobody in sales is running git log.

waves.title: Operational Transformation (algorithm behind Wave, Google Docs)
waves.creator: charlie@localhost

blips.author: charlie@localhost
lines: Good overview of operational transformation. The part worth rereading is transform():
two concurrent ops, each rewritten against the other, so both sites converge.
The proofs get hairy once you add more than insert and delete.

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: The client in our Emacs port only does insert, delete and retain, and that already took a day to get right around cursors.

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: Did you property-test it? Generate two random op lists, transform both ways, compare documents.

blips.author: charlie@localhost
lines: That is the TP1 property. Writing it down as a generator is maybe twenty lines; it found two bugs in mine.

waves.title: Google Wave Available for Everyone
waves.creator: bob@localhost

blips.author: bob@localhost
lines: No more invites needed, it is open to everyone now.
Making this one public so anyone on the server can find it.

blips.author: dave@localhost
lines: Good timing. The invite trading was getting silly.

blips.author: frank@localhost
lines: Anyone tried the robots API yet? I want one that summarizes a wave into a single blip at the end of the day.

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: I have a toy robot that tallies gadget votes. Happy to share the code.

blips.author: frank@localhost
lines: Please do. Robots that write back into the wave are the part I find most interesting.

waves.title: Google Kills Wave
waves.creator: alice@localhost

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: Development is ending at the end of the year. Export what you care about.
Added a poll below so we know who still needs help with exports.

blips.author: bob@localhost
lines: Not surprised, but sad. The protocol work deserved a longer life.

blips.author: charlie@localhost
lines: The protocol and the federation server are open source, so the ideas survive even if the product does not.

blips.author: dave@localhost
lines: That is the hopeful read. Someone will need to run the servers, though.

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: Which is more or less what this repository is: a client that still talks to a server we run ourselves.

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: Practical question: does export keep the reply structure, or does it flatten everything?

blips.author: frank@localhost
lines: It flattens. I wrote a small script that rebuilds the thread from the parent ids in the raw export.

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: Perfect, I will borrow that.

blips.author: bob@localhost
lines: One thing I will miss: watching someone type in a reply three levels deep and knowing exactly which point they were answering.

blips.author: dave@localhost
lines: Agreed. The tree was the right shape for discussion. Most chat tools still flatten it.

waves.title: Sandbox account arrived
waves.creator: frank@localhost

blips.author: frank@localhost
lines: Sandbox account arrived this morning. Testing whether the federation demo server accepts my client before I tell anyone.

waves.title: Eight Wave invites to give away
waves.creator: dave@localhost

blips.author: dave@localhost
lines: I have eight invites left. Reply here if you want one and I will send it tonight.

blips.author: charlie@localhost
lines: One for a colleague please, she does a lot of collaborative writing.

blips.author: dave@localhost
lines: Sent.

waves.title: Docker Sandboxes – Disposable, isolated sandboxes for AI agents
waves.creator: heidi@localhost

blips.author: heidi@localhost
lines: Disposable sandboxes per agent session. The interesting question is what crosses the boundary:
filesystem mounts, network egress, and credentials.
Isolation of the process is the easy part.

blips.author: bob@localhost
lines: Egress is where I keep getting surprised. An agent with no network but a package manager is an agent with a network.

blips.author: heidi@localhost
lines: Yes. Allowlist the registry mirror and nothing else, and log every denied connection so you can see what it tried.

blips.author: dave@localhost
lines: Logging denials has been the most useful signal for us. It tells you what the task actually needed.

blips.author: bob@localhost
lines: And it makes a good test: if the denial log is empty for a week, the allowlist is probably too wide.

blips.author: heidi@localhost
lines: I like that as a hardening trigger. Writing it down.

blips.author: dave@localhost
lines: How do you hand credentials in? Mounting a token file feels wrong but env vars leak into every child.

blips.author: heidi@localhost
lines: Short-lived tokens through a broker on a unix socket. The sandbox can ask; it cannot list or keep.

blips.author: bob@localhost
lines: That is the pattern I keep coming back to. Ask, do not hold.

blips.author: dave@localhost
lines: Startup time matters too. If a fresh sandbox takes thirty seconds, people will reuse them and lose the point.

blips.author: bob@localhost
lines: ZFS clones get us under a second on the jail side. Snapshot once, clone per session.

blips.author: heidi@localhost
lines: Nice. Disposable only works if it is cheap.

waves.title: Show HN: A context-aware permission guard for Claude Code
waves.creator: bob@localhost

blips.author: bob@localhost
lines: A permission guard that reads context before allowing a command. Curious how it decides.
A static allowlist misses intent; a model-based judge is hard to audit.

blips.author: heidi@localhost
lines: Hybrid seems right: deny-list for the obviously destructive, allow-list for read-only, and only ask about the middle.

blips.author: dave@localhost
lines: The middle is where all the work is. git push, writing outside the project, anything with curl.

blips.author: bob@localhost
lines: I would want every decision logged with the rule that matched, so I can tune it later.

blips.author: heidi@localhost
lines: Agreed. A guard you cannot explain is a guard you eventually turn off.

blips.author: dave@localhost
lines: Has anyone measured how many prompts per hour before people start approving everything?

blips.author: bob@localhost
lines: Anecdotally, about a dozen. After that every prompt is a yes.

waves.title: Escaping containment: A security analysis of FreeBSD jails [video]
waves.creator: dave@localhost

blips.author: dave@localhost
lines: Talk on escaping jails. Worth watching for the list of what is shared with the host by default.

blips.author: heidi@localhost
lines: Most of the findings were configuration, not kernel bugs. Raw sockets, devfs rules, and mounted host paths.

blips.author: bob@localhost
lines: Which is good news: those are all things a config linter can check.

blips.author: dave@localhost
lines: We should write that linter. Jail.conf in, list of risky settings out.

waves.title: Why Don't People Use Formal Methods?
waves.creator: grace@localhost

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: Classic question. My short answer: the spec is cheap, the habit is expensive.
Nobody budgets the week it takes to learn to think in states and transitions.

blips.author: charlie@localhost
lines: And the payoff is invisible. A bug that never ships does not get a postmortem.

blips.author: heidi@localhost
lines: We had one that would have. A TLA+ model of our lease protocol found a double-owner trace in an afternoon.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: That is the story that sells it. Did you keep the spec up to date afterwards?

blips.author: heidi@localhost
lines: For a while. It drifted once the code moved on. We now check it in next to the code and review them together.

blips.author: charlie@localhost
lines: Drift is the real cost. A spec nobody runs is just documentation.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: Lightweight tools help. Alloy gives you a counterexample in seconds, which keeps the loop tight.

blips.author: charlie@localhost
lines: Alloy for structure, TLA+ for behaviour over time. That split has worked for me.

blips.author: heidi@localhost
lines: Property tests are the gateway drug. Once people write invariants for tests, a model is a short step.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: Agreed. Same invariants, different checker.

waves.title: What TLA+ can and can't check
waves.creator: charlie@localhost

blips.author: charlie@localhost
lines: Useful reminder of the limits: TLC checks a finite model, not your system.
Small constants find most bugs, but small is not all.

blips.author: heidi@localhost
lines: And liveness needs fairness assumptions that are easy to get subtly wrong.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: Wrong fairness is the worst kind of wrong, because the checker happily says everything terminates.

blips.author: charlie@localhost
lines: I now add a deliberately broken variant of each spec and confirm the checker catches it. Cheap insurance.

blips.author: heidi@localhost
lines: Mutation testing for specs. Nice.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: Also: the refinement mapping to code is still on you. The model says nothing about the implementation unless you connect them.

waves.title: Dafny – A programming language with a program verifier
waves.creator: heidi@localhost

blips.author: heidi@localhost
lines: Dafny again. I like that the verifier runs as you type; it feels closer to a type checker than a proof assistant.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: Until the verifier times out and you are guessing which lemma it needs.

blips.author: charlie@localhost
lines: Splitting the method and asserting intermediate facts usually gets it unstuck. It is a bit like printf debugging for proofs.

blips.author: heidi@localhost
lines: Ha, yes. Assert, see if it holds, move the assert down.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: Has anyone compiled Dafny to something they shipped? I am curious about the generated code quality.

blips.author: charlie@localhost
lines: To C# and Go for small libraries. Readable enough to review, not something you would hand-edit.

waves.title: REPL-Driven Development (2017)
waves.creator: alice@localhost

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: The best description I know of why the REPL is a workflow and not a feature.
You grow the program while it runs, and the file is where you keep what worked.

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: The discipline is sending forms from the buffer, not typing into the REPL. Otherwise nothing ends up in the file.

blips.author: frank@localhost
lines: And restarting now and then to prove the file alone rebuilds the state you have been relying on.

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: Hidden state is the classic trap. Old definitions that no longer exist in source but still answer calls.

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: A clean reload on every test run catches most of it.

blips.author: frank@localhost
lines: Same story in Guile with Geiser. The tooling differs, the habit is identical.

waves.title: A History of Clojure [pdf]
waves.creator: frank@localhost

blips.author: frank@localhost
lines: The history paper is a great read. Immutable data by default and a careful story about state.
It is striking how few of the core decisions changed after the first public release.

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: Persistent collections were the bet that paid off. Everything else leans on them.

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: Plus atoms being the boring default. Most code never needs anything fancier.

blips.author: frank@localhost
lines: Agents and refs got less use than people expected, but having them there made the model coherent.

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: I have used refs exactly once in production, and it was the right tool that one time.

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: That is about the right rate for a sharp tool.

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: The section on hosting on the JVM is underrated. Reusing a platform let them skip a decade of runtime work.

blips.author: frank@localhost
lines: And ClojureScript repeated the trick on JavaScript.

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: What I would love is the same paper for spec: what problem it set out to solve and where it landed.

blips.author: frank@localhost
lines: I think the answer is: generative testing, more than validation.

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: Agreed, the generators are what I actually use it for.

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: Reading list for the weekend sorted, then.

waves.title: Optimizing Guile Scheme
waves.creator: ivan@localhost

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: Nice walkthrough of profiling Guile. The compiler does a lot if you let it see the types.

blips.author: frank@localhost
lines: The big win in the post was avoiding generic arithmetic in the inner loop. Same lesson as every Lisp.

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: Did they try the statprof module? It made a similar issue obvious for me in about five minutes.

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: They used it, yes. The flame graph was the clearest part of the post.

blips.author: frank@localhost
lines: Good to know the tooling is that mature now.

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: Saving this for the next time someone says Scheme is only for teaching.

waves.title: Unix v4 Tape Found
waves.creator: judy@localhost

blips.author: judy@localhost
lines: A Fourth Edition tape turned up. If it reads cleanly, it fills one of the bigger gaps in the early source history.

blips.author: frank@localhost
lines: Fourth Edition is the first kernel in C, if I remember right. Seeing that transition in source would be wonderful.

blips.author: dave@localhost
lines: The question is whether the tape is still readable after fifty years. Old oxide tends to shed.

blips.author: judy@localhost
lines: Apparently the plan is a careful bake and a flux-level read, then decode in software.

blips.author: bob@localhost
lines: Flux-level capture is the right call. You can rerun the decoder later as it improves.

blips.author: frank@localhost
lines: If it boots in an emulator I am clearing a weekend.

blips.author: judy@localhost
lines: Same. I already have a PDP-11 config ready from the earlier editions.

waves.title: PDP-11 Booting
waves.creator: dave@localhost

blips.author: dave@localhost
lines: Step by step boot of a PDP-11 from the front panel. Toggle in the bootstrap, then load the rest from disk.

blips.author: bob@localhost
lines: Toggling in a loader by hand is the best way I know to understand what a boot sector is for.

blips.author: judy@localhost
lines: And why the first loader was so small. Every word cost a row of switches.

blips.author: frank@localhost
lines: I did it once in an emulator with the panel simulated. Took three tries to get the address right.

blips.author: dave@localhost
lines: Octal everywhere helps once you are used to it. The instruction fields line up on octal digits.

blips.author: judy@localhost
lines: Saving this for the reading group.

waves.title: What Have We Learned from the PDP-11?
waves.creator: frank@localhost

blips.author: frank@localhost
lines: Good retrospective on what the PDP-11 taught later architectures.
Orthogonal addressing modes, memory-mapped I/O, and a stack that the instruction set actually used.
A lot of what C assumes about machines starts here.

blips.author: judy@localhost
lines: The autoincrement modes are the ones people always mention, and they really do shape idioms like *p++.

blips.author: dave@localhost
lines: Though the article is careful to say that may be coincidence more than design.

blips.author: frank@localhost
lines: Either way it fits the hardware nicely.

blips.author: judy@localhost
lines: The Unibus section was new to me. One bus for everything made adding devices very simple.

blips.author: dave@localhost
lines: And very slow once everything was on it. Every design pays somewhere.

waves.title: Hypothesis: Property-Based Testing for Python
waves.creator: erin@localhost

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: Hypothesis keeps getting better. Shrinking is still the feature that wins people over:
the failing case you see is small enough to read.

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: Integrated shrinking is the key design choice. You shrink the choices, not the values, so invariants survive.

blips.author: charlie@localhost
lines: Which is why custom generators shrink well for free. With the older approach you had to write a shrinker per type.

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: We have that exact pain in a Clojure codebase. Writing shrinkers by hand is nobody's favourite task.

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: test.check shrinks through bind as of a while ago, but it is still easier to get wrong.

blips.author: charlie@localhost
lines: The stateful testing module is my favourite part. Rules plus invariants, and it finds sequences you would never write.

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: We used it on a cache and it found an eviction bug after about forty operations. Shrunk to six.

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: Forty down to six is the whole pitch in one sentence.

waves.title: The sad state of property-based testing libraries
waves.creator: ivan@localhost

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: A fair survey: lots of languages have a property testing library, few have one with good shrinking and stateful tests.

blips.author: charlie@localhost
lines: Porting is hard because the good designs depend on internals of the runner, not just the generator API.

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: And because the hard part is invisible in a README. Two libraries look the same until a test fails.

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: Good test for a library: write a deliberately failing property and look at what it reports.

blips.author: charlie@localhost
lines: Agreed. If the counterexample is three hundred elements long, keep looking.

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: I would add: does it save failing examples between runs? That one feature saves hours.

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: The example database is underrated. It turns a flaky failure into a reproducible one.

blips.author: charlie@localhost
lines: Worth a mention in the article, I think.

waves.title: Mutation Driven Testing: When TDD Just Isn’t Good Enough
waves.creator: charlie@localhost

blips.author: charlie@localhost
lines: Mutation testing as a check on the tests rather than the code. Surviving mutants show you where assertions are missing.

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: The run time is the obstacle. Full mutation runs on a big suite take hours.

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: Running only on changed lines in CI brings it down to minutes for most changes.

blips.author: charlie@localhost
lines: That is what we do. Plus a weekly full run that files issues for the survivors.

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: Do you get many equivalent mutants? That was the noise that made us stop last time.

blips.author: charlie@localhost
lines: Some. We mark them once with a comment and the tool skips them after that.

waves.title: We should revisit literate programming in the agent era
waves.creator: grace@localhost

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: Interesting argument: if agents read and write most of the code, prose next to code becomes context, not decoration.
The explanation is the part the next reader, human or not, needs most.

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: I have seen this in practice. Org files with the reasoning next to each block give much better edits than bare source.

blips.author: judy@localhost
lines: Only if the prose stays true. Stale explanation is worse than none, for either kind of reader.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: Tangle checks help. If the source and the document disagree, the build fails.

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: We added a detangle check too, so edits made directly in the source flow back or get flagged.

blips.author: judy@localhost
lines: Both directions checked is the only setup I have seen survive more than a month.

blips.author: judy@localhost
lines: The older objection still stands: order for explanation and order for compilation differ, and tools have to reconcile them.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: Named blocks and noweb references solve it, at the price of a slightly odd reading experience.

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: I would read a follow-up with measurements. Edit quality with and without the prose, same tasks.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: That would make a nice experiment for one of our repos.

waves.title: Org-Mode Is One of the Most Reasonable Markup Languages to Use for Text
waves.creator: alice@localhost

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: Agree with most of this. Org markup is regular enough to read raw, which is the test I care about.

blips.author: judy@localhost
lines: The tables alone are worth it. Plain text that recalculates is still a small marvel.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: Spreadsheet formulas in a text file, under version control, with diffs you can read.

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: And export to HTML without a separate toolchain. The publishing story is the part people underestimate.

blips.author: judy@localhost
lines: Underestimate until a project has two hundred pages and the include paths start to matter.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: Ha. Our site build has a whole note on include patterns for that reason.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: The one fair criticism: outside Emacs the tooling is thin.

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: True, but the files remain readable without any tooling at all, which is a decent fallback.

blips.author: judy@localhost
lines: Bookmarking for the next markup discussion at work.

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: Bring the table demo. It wins people over every time.

waves.title: Literate programming: presenting code in human order
waves.creator: judy@localhost

blips.author: judy@localhost
lines: Short and clear piece: present code in the order a person needs to understand it, then let the tool reorder for the compiler.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: That reordering is the whole trick. Without it you are just writing long comments.

blips.author: alice@localhost
lines: And the reader gets the overview first, which most codebases never offer.

blips.author: judy@localhost
lines: I tried it for a small parser. The document read better than any parser I have written before.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: Did it stay that way after a few changes?

blips.author: judy@localhost
lines: Mostly. The tangle check made sure I updated the prose when I touched the code.

waves.title: Machine Learning Crash Course
waves.creator: ivan@localhost

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: A free crash course with exercises. Good for people who want the intuition before the maths.

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: The section on feature crosses was the clearest explanation I have read.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: And the bit on regularization. Everyone nods at L2 until they see the loss curves side by side.

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: The playground exercises carry most of it. Changing one slider and watching the boundary move is worth a chapter.

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: Interactive is the right format for this material.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: I would pair it with a statistics refresher. The course is light on why the metrics mean what they mean.

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: Fair. Precision and recall deserve more than one page.

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: Especially with imbalanced classes, which is every real dataset I have touched.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: Sharing with the new folks on the team.

waves.title: The First Rule of Machine Learning: Start Without Machine Learning
waves.creator: grace@localhost

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: Start without machine learning. A heuristic gives you a baseline and a pipeline, which you need anyway.

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: The pipeline is the real deliverable. The model is the last ten percent.

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: And the heuristic tells you whether the data even has signal before you spend a month on features.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: We shipped a rules version first once, and it was good enough that the model project quietly got cancelled.

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: That is a success story, even if nobody gets a paper out of it.

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: Best kind of project outcome, honestly.

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: The rule about monitoring before launch is the one I would underline. Most failures are silent drift.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: Log the inputs too, not just predictions. You cannot diagnose drift without them.

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: And keep a frozen sample to compare against every week.

waves.title: Scikit-Learn Version 1.0
waves.creator: erin@localhost

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: Version 1.0 after all these years. Keyword-only arguments and a cleaner API surface, mostly.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: The consistent fit and predict interface is still the best design decision in the ecosystem.

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: Pipelines plus grid search on top of that interface is how most of my projects start.

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: And end, honestly. A gradient boosted model in a pipeline covers a lot of tabular problems.

blips.author: grace@localhost
lines: Tabular data is still where classic methods win most of the time.

blips.author: ivan@localhost
lines: Nice to see the version number finally match how stable it has been.

blips.author: erin@localhost
lines: Agreed. It has felt like a 1.0 for a long time.
